articles.title: Voyager 2 was running out of power. NASA just bought it more time
articles.summary: NASA engineers have found a clever way to squeeze more life out of Voyager 2, nearly half a century after it left Earth. In an operation nicknamed the “Big Bang,” the team simultaneously shut down certain power-hungry hardware and switched to lower-power alternatives while keeping the spacecraft warm enough to survive.
articles.content:
NASA engineers have found a way to free up additional power aboard Voyager 2, helping the nearly 50-year-old spacecraft continue its scientific work for longer.

The effort, known as the "Big Bang," was carried out by engineers at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory. The team simultaneously shut down certain powered components and replaced them with options that use less energy, while also making sure Voyager 2 stayed warm enough to function properly.

Voyager 2's Shrinking Power Supply

Voyager 2 and its twin, Voyager 1, rely on radioisotope thermoelectric generators, which produce electricity from heat released by decaying plutonium. As that plutonium supply steadily diminishes, each spacecraft loses about 4 watts of available power every year.

After nearly half a century in space, the Voyagers now have extremely limited power to spare. To keep the spacecraft operating, mission controllers have increasingly had to shut down systems and equipment that are no longer essential.

Since 2024, declining power levels have forced the team to switch off two science instruments on each Voyager spacecraft (each spacecraft has 10 instruments; others had been turned off previously because they were only used for the mission's planetary encounters).

An Extra Year of Science

Without the "Big Bang" power saving effort, the Voyager team would have needed to turn off another instrument aboard Voyager 2 before the end of 2026. The newly freed power is expected to keep the spacecraft's three remaining instruments operating for at least one additional year.

NASA plans to carry out the same power-saving swap on Voyager 1, which is currently farther from Earth than Voyager 2. The mission team expects to complete that work in the coming months.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant and inspiring achievement by NASA engineers who have extended the operational life of Voyager 2, a nearly 50-year-old spacecraft, through an innovative power-saving strategy. This breakthrough allows continued scientific exploration and data collection from deep space, benefiting humanity's understanding of the universe. The impact is broad, meaningful, and well-detailed, focusing on a single important topic.
articles.personality_title: NASA extends Voyager 2’s mission with clever power-saving fix
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Voyager 2 is a spacecraft launched nearly 50 years ago to explore space beyond our solar system. It runs on power from a special battery that slowly loses energy over time.

**What happened** – NASA engineers found a smart way to save power on Voyager 2 by turning off some equipment that uses a lot of energy and switching to parts that need less power. This operation, called the “Big Bang,” also made sure the spacecraft stayed warm enough to keep working.

**Impact** – This power-saving trick gives Voyager 2 about one more year to keep sending back valuable scientific information from deep space. Without this effort, the spacecraft would have had to turn off more instruments and stop collecting some data by 2026.

**What's next step** – NASA plans to do the same power-saving changes on Voyager 1, the twin spacecraft of Voyager 2, in the next few months to help it keep working longer.

**One-sentence takeaway** – NASA’s smart power-saving changes are allowing the nearly 50-year-old Voyager 2 to continue exploring space and sending important data for at least one more year.

articles.title: Earth extremophile can grow in near-Mars-like conditions
articles.summary: A salt-loving microorganism found in places like the Dead Sea can not just survive but actively grow in conditions close to those that may be found just under the Martian surface
articles.content:
A salt-loving microorganism found in places like the Dead Sea can not just survive but actively grow in conditions close to those that may be found just under the Martian surface

A view of Mars’s surface captured by the Perseverance rover NASA/JPL-Caltech/ASU/MSS​S

We have found tantalising hints that not only was there once life on Mars, but that it might still exist on the Red Planet. Now, a study here on Earth has made that idea more plausible by showing that salt-loving, or halophilic, microbes can grow in conditions close to those that might be found in little pockets of highly salty water just below the surface of Mars.

“We show that these halophilic microorganisms can actively grow under a combination of anoxic [oxygen-free], low-pressure atmosphere conditions and a high-salt liquid media that contains harmful Martian chemicals that are similar to bleach, which are the perchlorates,” says Adam Robinson at the University of Florida. “And that’s something that nobody had been able to show before.”

Robinson and his colleagues designed their experiments based on the idea that there might be pockets of liquid, salty water just below the surface of Mars. We haven’t found any, says Robinson, but work by other researchers suggests they might exist.

Advertisement

The microbe used in the experiments is Haloferax volcanii, an archaeon – the other kind of simple cell besides bacteria – that thrives in extremely salty waters such as the Dead Sea. It’s relatively easy to grow compared with many other microbes that live in extreme environments, known as extremophiles.

The team put these microbes in water containing 225 grams of salt per litre, and kept it at a temperature of 21°C (about 70°F) and a pressure of 24 millibar for 160 days. Varying levels of nitrates and chlorates were added to different batches. For controls, the microbes were grown in the same media but at Earth atmospheric pressure: 1013 millibar.

Free newsletter Sign up to Launchpad Sign up to newsletter

While growth was slower in the low-pressure condition, it did still occur, as shown by the growth medium becoming cloudier – a standard measure of growth – and the biological reduction of nitrate and perchlorate. A scanning electron microscope also revealed extensive biofilm formation.

“So there’s pretty robust evidence that points towards active growth and not just survival,” says Robinson. Many previous studies have demonstrated that microbes can survive in Mars-like conditions, he says, but very few have shown growth, and none have shown growth of salt-loving extremophiles.

But do pockets of salty water really exist under the Martian surface? We don’t know, in part because since the Viking missions in 1976 found possible signs of life, other missions have avoided the most promising areas, says Robinson. “They specifically avoided places that were deemed potentially habitable, because we don’t want to contaminate regions where there might be life with our own spacecraft and landers.”

It is surprising that any Earth microbe can grow in these conditions at all, says team member Scott Perl at the Los Angeles Natural History Museum, given that nowhere on Earth’s surface has such low pressure. But if life did evolve on Mars billions of years ago, when conditions were more favourable, it would have had ample time to adapt to such conditions, he says.

However, the pressure and temperature combination used might be higher than those found on Mars, and the team did add yeast extract to the growth medium as a carbon source. “So the growth medium is Mars-like in the sense that it has high salinity and the chlorates and nitrates in it. But it’s not Mars-like in the sense that we’re giving a complex carbon source that would not be found on Mars today,” says Robinson. “It’s a starting point for future experiments.”

In these experiments, the team plans to replace the yeast abstract with acetate, a potential carbon source thought to be found on Mars today.

Sean McMahon at the University of Edinburgh, UK, says that temperatures on the surface of Mars can exceed 21°C during the day. “But here, the pressure is only around 6 to 12 millibar. The difference is significant because, in the realistic range, water cannot stay liquid. No liquid water, no life.”

Below the surface where pressures could reach 24 millibar, the temperatures are well below freezing, says McMahon.

Robinson thinks the conditions used in the study are plausible on Mars. But the team is already investigating whether cold-loving halophiles can grow at temperatures of between 0 and 4°C (32 and 39°F) and pressures of between 7 and 12 millibar, he says.

There is also the issue of what lasting food source there could be for microbes on Mars. The most likely source is the carbon dioxide in the atmosphere – microbes called methanogens can feed on CO2 and spew out methane, which has been detected on Mars. There are a few salt-loving methanogens on Earth, says Robinson, which the team hopes to try to grow in Mars-like conditions.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific breakthrough showing that salt-loving microbes can actively grow in near-Mars-like conditions, supporting the possibility of extant life on Mars. This has broad implications for astrobiology and our understanding of life beyond Earth, providing hopeful and inspiring insights into planetary science and the search for extraterrestrial life. The study is detailed and focused on a single important topic with clear experimental context and future research directions.
articles.personality_title: Salt-loving microbe grows in conditions similar to Mars underground
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Scientists have wondered if life could exist beneath the surface of Mars, where salty water might be trapped in tiny pockets. Mars is a cold planet with very low air pressure, and its surface has chemicals that can be harmful to life as we know it.

**What happened** – Researchers at the University of Florida tested a salt-loving microbe called Haloferax volcanii, which lives in very salty places on Earth like the Dead Sea. They put this microbe in salty water with chemicals like those on Mars and kept it in low-pressure, oxygen-free conditions similar to what might exist below Mars’s surface. Over 160 days, the microbe not only survived but grew, forming groups called biofilms.

**Impact** – This is the first time scientists have shown that salt-loving microbes can actively grow—not just survive—in conditions close to those possibly found on Mars. It means that if similar salty water pockets exist on Mars, life might be able to live there too. This finding supports the idea that life could still exist on Mars underground.

**What's next step** – The researchers plan to test if microbes can grow in even colder temperatures and lower pressures like those deeper on Mars. They also want to try growing microbes that use carbon sources found on Mars today, such as carbon dioxide, to better understand if life could survive there long-term.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A salt-loving microbe from Earth can grow in Mars-like salty, low-pressure conditions, suggesting life might survive below Mars’s surface.
articles.personality_title_fr: Un microbe aimant le sel pousse dans des conditions proches de celles sous la surface de Mars
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les scientifiques se demandent si la vie pourrait exister sous la surface de Mars, où de petites poches d’eau salée pourraient être piégées. Mars est une planète froide avec une très faible pression atmosphérique, et sa surface contient des produits chimiques qui peuvent être nocifs pour la vie telle que nous la connaissons.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des chercheurs de l’Université de Floride ont testé un microbe aimant le sel appelé Haloferax volcanii, qui vit dans des endroits très salés sur Terre comme la Mer Morte. Ils ont placé ce microbe dans de l’eau salée contenant des produits chimiques semblables à ceux de Mars, en conditions de basse pression et sans oxygène, proches de celles qui pourraient exister sous la surface martienne. Pendant 160 jours, le microbe a non seulement survécu, mais a aussi grandi en formant des biofilms.

**Impact** – C’est la première fois que des scientifiques montrent que des microbes aimant le sel peuvent réellement croître – pas seulement survivre – dans des conditions proches de celles que l’on trouve peut-être sur Mars. Cela signifie que si des poches d’eau salée similaires existent sur Mars, la vie pourrait y survivre. Cette découverte soutient l’idée que la vie pourrait encore exister sous la surface de Mars.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs prévoient de tester si des microbes peuvent croître à des températures plus froides et sous des pressions plus basses, comme celles trouvées plus profondément sur Mars. Ils veulent aussi essayer de faire pousser des microbes qui utilisent des sources de carbone présentes aujourd’hui sur Mars, comme le dioxyde de carbone, pour mieux comprendre si la vie peut y survivre sur le long terme.

**Conclusion en une phrase** – Un microbe terrestre aimant le sel peut croître dans des conditions salées et de basse pression proches de Mars, suggérant que la vie pourrait survivre sous sa surface.
articles.personality_title_es: Un microbio amante de la sal crece en condiciones similares a las del subsuelo de Marte
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los científicos se preguntan si podría existir vida bajo la superficie de Marte, donde podrían encontrarse pequeñas bolsas de agua salada. Marte es un planeta frío con muy baja presión atmosférica, y su superficie tiene químicos que pueden ser dañinos para la vida tal como la conocemos.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores de la Universidad de Florida probaron un microbio amante de la sal llamado Haloferax volcanii, que vive en lugares muy salados de la Tierra como el Mar Muerto. Pusieron este microbio en agua salada con químicos similares a los de Marte, en condiciones de baja presión y sin oxígeno, parecidas a las que podrían existir bajo la superficie marciana. Durante 160 días, el microbio no solo sobrevivió, sino que creció formando grupos llamados biofilms.

**Impacto** – Es la primera vez que los científicos muestran que microbios amantes de la sal pueden crecer activamente —no solo sobrevivir— en condiciones parecidas a las de Marte. Esto significa que si existen bolsas similares de agua salada en Marte, la vida podría sobrevivir allí. Este hallazgo apoya la idea de que la vida podría seguir existiendo bajo la superficie de Marte.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores planean probar si los microbios pueden crecer a temperaturas más frías y presiones más bajas, como las que hay más profundo en Marte. También quieren intentar cultivar microbios que usen fuentes de carbono que se encuentran en Marte hoy, como el dióxido de carbono, para entender mejor si la vida podría sobrevivir a largo plazo.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Un microbio terrestre amante de la sal puede crecer en condiciones salinas y de baja presión similares a las de Marte, lo que sugiere que la vida podría sobrevivir bajo su superficie.
